message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This study is unusually well grounded for a capital request because we did not rely on vendor brochures. We insisted on a three-day trial with our own cases and pallet patterns, and the results show the cell sustaining at least 14 cases a minute, above our 12-a-minute line rate, so throughput risk is retired. The financial case is built from our actual labour costs and a firm vendor quote, and it pays back in 3.4 years against a four-year hurdle, with redeployment to Line 5 for every displaced operator. Just as important to me is the safety case. We have our own evidence on site: Line 3, which is already automated, had 4 manual-handling injuries last year against 11 on Lines 1 and 2, which shows clearly what automation does for injury rates. Palletising is the hardest job in the plant, and this removes it. I have reviewed the risks around changeovers and pallet quality and both are manageable. This is a sound investment on cost, capacity and safety grounds.
</author>

<document>
Feasibility Study: Robotic Palletising on Lines 1 and 2
Operations Engineering, Kestrel Foods, Wrexley Plant, February 2026

1. Purpose
This study assesses whether to replace manual palletising at the end of packing Lines 1 and 2 with two robotic palletising cells, and recommends a course of action to the Plant Investment Board.

2. Current operation
Lines 1 and 2 pack savoury snacks into cases, which are stacked onto pallets by hand at the end of each line. Each line has two palletising operators per shift, and the lines run two shifts a day (06:00-14:00 and 14:00-22:00), five days a week. That is eight operator posts in total. At a fully loaded cost of £36,500 per operator per year, manual palletising costs £292,000 a year.

Palletising is the most physically demanding task on site. Operators lift around 4,000 cases per shift, and the task accounts for most of our manual-handling injuries.

Under the site plan agreed by the Board in December 2025, Lines 1 and 2 will move to a single day shift from January 2027, as volume consolidates onto the new high-speed Line 5.

3. The proposed solution
Each cell consists of a four-axis robot, a layer-forming conveyor, a pallet dispenser, safety guarding and a stretch-wrapper. One operator per shift would supervise both cells, handle pallet changes and clear faults.

Vendor trial
The preferred vendor ran a three-day trial in January using our actual cases and pallet patterns.

Table 1. Vendor trial results, 12-14 January 2026
Case type | Share of Line 1 and 2 volume | Peak rate (cases/min) | Sustained rate over 8 hours (cases/min)
14 kg catering case | 60% | 13 | 10.5
8 kg retail case | 40% | 16 | 14.0

Our lines run at up to 12 cases per minute. The trial confirmed that the cell sustains at least 14 cases per minute across our case types, comfortably above our line rate, so the cell will not become a bottleneck.

4. Safety benefit
Line 3 has had an automated case packer and palletiser since 2023. In 2025 it recorded 4 manual-handling injuries, compared with 11 across Lines 1 and 2. Automation clearly reduces injuries, and we expect robotic palletising to cut manual-handling injuries on Lines 1 and 2 by a similar proportion. For context, Line 3 runs the lighter 6 kg multipack cases and operates on a single shift.

5. Costs and savings
Table 2. Financial summary
Item | Amount
Capital: two cells, installed, including guarding and conveyors | £620,000
Annual maintenance contract (two cells) | £36,000
Remaining supervision: one operator per shift, two shifts | £73,000 per year
Current manual palletising cost | £292,000 per year
Net annual saving (£292,000 - £73,000 - £36,000) | £183,000
Simple payback (£620,000 / £183,000) | 3.4 years

The Plant Investment Board's hurdle for automation projects is a payback of four years or less, so the project meets the hurdle with a margin. The three operators displaced on each shift would be offered redeployment to Line 5, which is currently recruiting.

6. Implementation
The vendor quotes a 16-week lead time. Installation would take place during the planned two-week August shutdown, with a further two weeks of commissioning at reduced line speed. We would train two engineering technicians on robot maintenance as part of the contract.

7. Risks
Changeovers to new case sizes require reprogramming, which the vendor will provide for the first year. Pallet quality varies between suppliers, and poor pallets cause faults in automated dispensing; we will tighten our pallet specification before go-live.

8. Recommendation
Robotic palletising on Lines 1 and 2 is technically proven on our own products, removes our most injurious manual task and pays back in 3.4 years, within the Board's four-year hurdle. We recommend the Board approve capital of £620,000 for installation in the August 2026 shutdown.
</document>
response:
# Review: Robotic Palletising Feasibility Study, Lines 1 and 2

The study's foundations are good: an on-site trial with your own cases, real labour costs, and a firm quote. But the document's own data contradicts all three of its headline claims. A Board reviewer who reads the tables closely will find each of these problems, so they need fixing before submission.

## 1. Throughput risk is not retired

The text says the cell "sustains at least 14 cases per minute across our case types." Table 1 shows that only the 8 kg retail case reached 14.0. The **14 kg catering case sustained 10.5 cases/min**, below your 12/min line rate. Even its peak of 13 is barely above line rate. That case is **60% of volume**, so the cell would be the bottleneck for most of your production whenever the line runs catering cases at full speed.

There may be a fair counter-argument. 4,000 cases per shift is about 8.3 cases/min on average, so actual demand may sit below 10.5 with some buffering. If that's true, make the argument explicitly with catering-case line speeds and accumulation capacity. As written, the claim is simply incorrect, and the trial actually points to throughput on heavy cases as the **main technical risk**, not a retired one.

## 2. The financial case ignores the Board's own shift plan

Section 2 notes that Lines 1 and 2 move to a **single day shift from January 2027**, but Table 2 costs everything on two shifts. With installation in August 2026, the cells would see only a few months of two-shift running, part of it during commissioning.

Restated on a single shift:

| Item | Two shifts (as submitted) | Single shift (from Jan 2027) |
|---|---|---|
| Manual palletising avoided | £292,000 | £146,000 (4 posts) |
| Remaining supervision | -£73,000 | -£36,500 |
| Maintenance contract | -£36,000 | -£36,000* |
| **Net annual saving** | **£183,000** | **£73,500** |
| **Simple payback** | **3.4 years** | **~8.4 years** |

\*Assumes the contract cost doesn't scale with hours; confirm with the vendor.

On the Board's own plan, the project **fails the four-year hurdle by a wide margin**. Half the claimed saving comes from the shift reduction that is already agreed, not from automation.

There are also costs missing from Table 2:
- reprogramming after the first year
- the tighter pallet specification
- lost output during two weeks of reduced-speed commissioning
- technician time

Each one lengthens payback further.

## 3. The Line 3 comparison doesn't support the safety claim

Comparing 4 injuries against 11 isn't like-for-like, as the study's own footnote shows:
- Line 3 is **one line on one shift**. Lines 1 and 2 are **two lines on two shifts**, about four times the exposure.
- Line 3 handles **6 kg** cases. Lines 1 and 2 handle 8 kg and 14 kg cases.

Normalised per line-shift, Line 3 has **4** injuries against **2.75** on Lines 1 and 2. On this data, the automated line looks *worse*, not better. The comparison also doesn't say how many of the 11 injuries were palletising-related.

The underlying point is probably still right: removing 4,000 lifts per shift of 8 to 14 kg cases very likely reduces musculoskeletal risk. But support it with your incident records broken down by task, or a manual-handling risk assessment of the palletising role, not the Line 3 figures. A well-evidenced safety case might justify the project on its own merits even with a longer payback, and that would be a more honest framing than forcing it through the payback hurdle.

## 4. Smaller points

- **Timing:** The plan targets the August 2026 shutdown, which has now passed. If this is still going to the Board, the next window almost certainly falls after the single-shift change, so the two-shift figures no longer apply at all.
- **Risks section:** "Manageable" needs owners and costs. Who reprograms changeovers in year two and beyond, and at what rate? What does the tighter pallet spec cost per pallet?
- **Redeployment:** This is reasonable, but the Line 5 consolidation may absorb these operators regardless. Make sure the baseline doesn't count a reduction that would happen anyway.

## Bottom line

The recommendation doesn't currently follow from the evidence. The trial shows a throughput shortfall on 60% of volume, the payback is about 8.4 years under the agreed single-shift plan, and the safety comparison is confounded. Before resubmitting, I'd suggest:

1. Asking the vendor about a higher-capacity cell or gripper for the 14 kg case, or modelling buffering explicitly.
2. Rebuilding the financials on single-shift operation, including all costs.
3. Rebuilding the safety case from task-level injury data and presenting it as a primary justification, possibly alongside a request for a hurdle exception.
